title: X-Automate brings physical and agentic AI to the lab | Xaira Therapeutics
content: Xaira’s ambition is to develop 10× more medicines for 10× more patients within 10 years . Our X-Suite connects AI models, scientific agents and experimental capabilities to accelerate that work. But biological discovery still depends on making and testing molecules in the lab. As automated production scales, downstream instruments can become the bottleneck: they often need a person to open a door, load a plate or start an instrument run. X-Automate is our laboratory automation system. It includes automation workcells for scaling up laboratory operations; X-Bot, our vision-guided, six-degree-of-freedom robotic arm built in-house using low-cost commercial hardware, and X-Scientist, Xaira’s agentic AI, which we introduced two days ago. X-Scientist uses a vision-language model (VLM) to interpret the scene, select operations, and coordinate workflows. In a seven-day HPLC demonstration, the system autonomously retrieved, transported, and analyzed 18 plates, 80% more than a modeled weekday 9-to-5 loading schedule. Recent results from X-Design, our AI for antibody design, show progress toward de novo generation of antibodies that can rapidly advance to therapeutic development. A compelling design must still prove itself experimentally: does it bind the intended target with appropriate selectivity and biological activity and have the properties needed for further development? We routinely make candidate proteins thousands at a time, then characterize them and verify their quality. Those measurements help project teams decide what to advance and to generate data that can improve our models. Faster design in turn demands faster validation, as the time between creating designs in silico and reliable experimental answers becomes a constraint on the whole cycle. Our standard industrial workcells automate protein expression and purification with a throughput of thousands of samples per week. But other analytical instruments in the lab still involve manual doors, drawers and software controls. They occupy crowded spaces, and need to be managed by human scientists. A plate of samples that becomes ready after just a few hours may frequently have to wait until morning or through a weekend for the next step in its processing. Automating conventional analytical instruments requires two capabilities: robotic arms that can interact with instruments built for people, and safeguards that support effective operation alongside scientists. Within X-Automate, X-Bot handles the physical interactions, while X-Scientist coordinates the workflow and safety safeguards. We built X-Bot, our vision-guided robotics platform, in-house to meet the needs of our scientists and laboratory workflows. Our first case study focuses on automating HPLC, the first bottleneck in our protein-production pipeline. Long per-sample analysis times require continuous operation, including outside standard work hours, to keep pace with the industrial workcell’s protein-production throughput. To build X-Bot, we paired an inexpensive, off-the-shelf six-degree-of-freedom robotic arm with open-source tools and developed the control and integration software in-house. We also machined metal gripper fingers in our machine shop and 3D-printed custom components to complete the hardware. Much of this work created reusable infrastructure, including the robotic controller, monitoring system and software interfaces. Adapting X-Bot to additional instruments still requires configuration and testing, but this foundation allows deployment within a few weeks, rather than the many months that a new development effort could require. The Agilent HPLC presents several challenges for commercial lab robots that rely on pre-taught positions. It lacks a motorized sample door, its plate tray allows little margin for placement error, and its drawer can shift at the slightest touch during pick-and-place operations. Software integration poses an additional barrier: access to its automation API requires an expensive license. X-Bot addresses the physical handling challenges with an arm-mounted camera that locates targets and estimates their orientation. Continuous visual feedback allows the arm to adjust its approach as it moves, even when the target shifts. In our demonstrations, the same pickup command handles plates in their usual position as well as rotated or tilted, without requiring a new pose to be taught for each configuration (Figure 1a & b). The arm also adapts if the HPLC drawer shifts during loading or unloading (Figure 1c & d). Figure 1. Physical handling and safeguards in one view. Recorded demonstrations show adaptive pickup (a & b), HPLC load and unloading with drawer displacement (c & d), intrusion monitoring (e), and response to lost camera data (f). Panels are independently time-compressed; the montage does not represent response timing. A separate overhead camera and computer monitor the space around the arm.
